citations.F1: `serialize_event` issues one `SELECT ... FROM users` per event, so limit=1000 means 1,000 round trips per request; fetch the distinct actor_ids in one `WHERE id = ANY($1)` query
citations.F2: `seen` is a list and `ev["dedupe_key"] in seen` is a linear scan per row; make it a `set`
citations.F3: `lookup_geo` uses `requests.get` (2 s timeout) inside an `async def` handler, so every cache-miss event stalls the whole worker's event loop
citations.F4: `events` has indexes only on `actor_id` and `kind`, so filtering org_id over 4.2M rows is a sequential scan; add `events (org_id, created_at DESC)`
citations.F5: the timing middleware appends one float per request on *every* route at ~120 req/s, so ~8.6M entries accumulate in 20 h; replace with a bounded `collections.deque(maxlen=N)`
citations.F6: `_geo_cache` also grows forever — keyed on raw client IP with no eviction and no bound; give it an LRU with a size cap
citations.F7: `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)` the slow query with org 4127 and the 30 d bound, and record p50/p95 from Datadog plus pod RSS slope as the baseline you will re-check after each change
citations.F9: Do not ship the on-call proposal — 16 workers × pool max 50 × 6 pods is up to 4,800 Postgres connections ... and a 60 s Redis cache leaves every miss blocking the event loop exactly as now
citations.F10: Attribute the remaining RSS before calling the leak fixed — run `tracemalloc` (or `pympler`) on a pod for an hour; the two unbounded structures should account for most of the 310 MB → 2.1 GB climb, and if they don't, something else is retaining
